newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico is model of good behavior after elections.
newsitem.headline: Mexico is model of good behavior after elections.

text.p: Mexico, a country once rife with post-electoral bickering, is bending over backwards to be civilised after landmark mid-term elections on July 6.

President Ernesto Zedillo, having steered the country through its cleanest elections ever, has barely stopped grinning for a week despite unprecedented electoral losses by his Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

His former foes on the left are seeking to shake off a rowdy image and have been models of good behaviour since the elections shot them to prominence as Mexico's second strongest party in the Chamber of Deputies.

The image of harmony was stamped on the front of every Mexico City newspaper on Tuesday: leftist leader Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, persona non grata in the presidential mansion for the last 10 years, smiling and shaking hands there with a beaming Zedillo.

Cardenas won a landslide victory in the first race in modern times for mayor of Mexico City, and his Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) stunned pundits by seizing the second biggest cluster of seats in the lower house of Congress.

On Tuesday, PRD leader Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador lectured a roomful of 125 party deputies, including actors, housewives, an aerobics teacher and a bus driver, all swept into power by an unexpected groundswell of support for the left.

His message, delivered in a schoolmasterly tone, was of strict responsibility to a party that has at times acted undecorously in Congress, heckling the president during his annual state of the nation address and donning pig-like facemasks to poke fun at his party.

"The conduct of our legislators must be guided by republican morality, with respect for opponents," Lopez Obrador said. "For that, we do not need raucous behaviour or shouting ... Firmness and political urbanity are enough."

In the presidential mansion of Los Pinos, Zedillo issued similar orders for his own party to behave itself following the loss of its majority in the lower house, which it had held for 68 years. He urged it to help broker a smooth transition.
"It is our duty to head this political evolution without reticence, without rupture, and without jeopardising stability and social peace," Zedillo told PRI party chiefs on Tuesday.
The political honeymoon could come to a quick end when the new Congress begins in September and the opposition in the lower house exercises its new powers on issues like the budget.

The blossoming harmony between the PRD and a PRI president contrasted sharply with an almost war-like attitude of the past decade. Violent PRD protests followed most local elections and party leaders branded as radicals by the PRI were shunned from the circles of power.
Cardenas, who had been a tireless campaigner against PRI electoral fraud for years, spoke warmly of Zedillo late on Monday, thanking him for his support since the elections.

Zedillo, in turn, told Cardenas during their first face-to-face meeting that he would be allowed to pick his own city police chief and attorney general -- powers still nominally under presidential authority.

In a startling move last week, Zedillo -- a former central banker and fervent free-market economist -- also came close to publically embracing the PRD. He said he had always believed a strong left-wing was in Mexico's interests.
